findings.problem: The one decision round 10 changed is spent through a single ground-blind alpha, and it only survives on one of the two grounds. Composited and measured against the .b-field it stands on: on paper the rail is rgb(167,162,242) at 2.30:1 while an ordinary --fore-16 hairline (.b-behind border-top, .b-bar border-bottom, .b-foot border-top) is 1.41:1 — the accent reads 1.63x stronger than a plain rule, which is what makes it read as structure. On ink the same declaration composites to rgb(48,44,123) at 1.587:1 while --fore-16 there is 1.588:1. The accent rail and an ordinary hairline are the same strength to three significant figures on the ink ground, so 'indigo draws the part of the rail that is still ahead' is a statement the dark room does not make — only a faint chroma shift distinguishes the spine of the instrument from the section rules. Note the two ratified indigo objects are NOT halved on either ground: .b-todayRule (b.css:101) and .b-item[data-lead="true"] .b-tick (b.css:298) both paint the accent at full strength, 3.00:1 on ink. The rail is the only indigo on the surface that is dimmed, and it is dimmed by the same amount on a ground where indigo has half the headroom. 0.5 is also not on the declared alpha ladder (0.90 / 0.72 / 0.62 / 0.46 / 0.28 / 0.16 / 0.10 / 0.06 / 0.04), and audit.mjs cannot see it: the palette lock (audit.mjs:196-211) matches the declared rgb triple within +/-1 and never reads alpha or opacity, so an undeclared tint of an allowed hue passes on both grounds.
findings.fix: Key the rail's alpha to the ground the way every other tone in the lab already is. Replace b.css:584 with two rules: `[data-accent="structure"] .b-rail { background: var(--accent); opacity: 0.46; }` and, immediately after it, `[data-ground="ink"][data-accent="structure"] .b-rail { opacity: 1; }` (data-ground and data-accent sit on the same element — body in the master, #deck in the console — so the compound selector is (0,3,0) and wins). That puts paper at 2.14:1 on a declared step, and ink at 3.00:1, the same full-strength indigo the today rule and the lead tick already use on that ground. Add the assertion first and watch it fail: in interaction-check.mjs, on both ?v=paper and ?v=ink, read getComputedStyle('.b-measure:not(.b-back) .b-rail') and require the composited rail-to-field contrast to be at least 1.5x the composited --fore-16 hairline contrast on the same ground.

findings.element: b.css:584 selector scope vs b.css:549-570 (.b-back) and interaction-check.mjs:1552-1564
findings.problem: [data-accent="structure"] .b-rail is unscoped, and .b-back is a .b-measure, so the rule paints the PAST rail too. On state=day — the wedding morning, the one screen the company is judged by — there is no forward measure at all: `document.querySelectorAll('.b-rail').length === 1` and that single rail is the past. Driven at 390 and 1440 on ?v=paper and ?v=ink, opening 'Behind you' reveals nine months of closed history drawn down an indigo spine, background rgb(79,70,229) at opacity 0.5 on both grounds. That contradicts three separate statements of intent: b.css:552-553 says of this exact block 'Quieter than what is ahead, and carrying no accent - nothing behind you is the next thing'; elevate.config.json's variantsLead says indigo is spent on 'the next thing AND the rail that is still ahead'; and the round note defines structure as the rail 'that is still ahead'. Neither gate can see it. audit.mjs walks only visible elements and the disclosure is closed at rest, so the past rail is never in a graded frame. And the behaviour gate's assertion that claims to guard precisely this — interaction-check.mjs:1564, ok('nothing behind you is the next thing', !back.accent) — defines `accent` at line 1552-1555 as any .b-tick whose backgroundColor is rgb(79,70,229). It tests ticks only. It has passed over an indigo past rail every run since the room changed.
findings.fix: Scope the accent to what is ahead. Immediately after b.css:584 add `[data-accent="structure"] .b-back .b-rail { background: var(--fore-16); opacity: 1; }` — (0,3,0) beats (0,2,0), it restores the base .b-rail tint declared at b.css:146, and it is above the forced-colours block at b.css:1547 so that block still wins where it must. Then widen the inert assertion: at interaction-check.mjs:1552 replace the tick-only `accent` probe with one that also reads getComputedStyle(measure.querySelector('.b-rail')).backgroundColor and fails if it is rgb(79,70,229), and run it on both ?v=paper and ?v=ink. Write the assertion first; it fails today.

findings.element: render-b.js:1012-1017 div.b-editGroup — span#b-vis.b-label + div.b-seg; .b-editGroup has zero rules in b.css
findings.problem: The editor has three field groups. Two of them carry an inline style="display:grid;gap:6px" (render-b.js:950 and :976) and stack their label above their control with a measured 6px of air. The third, the visibility group, was given a class name and never a rule — grep .b-editGroup across b.css returns 0 matches — so it lands as display:block with an inline span.b-label and an inline-flex div.b-seg sharing one line box. The h() builder inserts no whitespace text node between siblings, so there is not even a word space. Measured with a Range over the label's text content against the segment's border box at 390, 768, 1024, 1152, 1279 and 1440, on ?v=paper and ?v=ink: the gap is 0.0px at every width on both grounds. The result is visible in a frame this panel has been shooting for rounds — shots/paper-owner-editing--390x844.png — where the final E of 'WHAT GUESTS SEE' runs flush into the filled black 'Shown' plate, so the label reads as part of the control rather than as its name. It also breaks the file's own --gap-control token, declared at shell.css:101-107 as the single name for 'the relationship between controls standing in a row': here that relationship is zero, under no name at all.
findings.fix: Give .b-editGroup the layout its two siblings have. Add to b.css, beside the other editor rules (after .b-seg at b.css:836): `.b-editGroup { display: grid; gap: var(--gap-hair); justify-items: start; }`. That stacks 'What guests see' above the Shown/Hidden plate on the declared 4px step, matches the two groups above it, and keeps the plate at its natural width because justify-items:start stops the grid item stretching (the existing .b-edit .b-seg { justify-self: start } at b.css:1407 only fires below 1024). While there, move the two inline `gap:6px` declarations in render-b.js:950 and :976 to the same token so all three groups sit on one step. Assertion to write first: at every graded width and on both grounds, the bounding box of #b-vis and the bounding box of .b-seg must not share a line box, and the vertical gap between them must equal getComputedStyle of the same pair in the 'What it is' group.

findings.problem: CSS generated content is part of the accessible name in Chromium, so the typographic open/closed mark is spoken. Read from the CDP accessibility tree on ?v=paper: state=phone gives DisclosureTriangle name 'BEHIND YOU 3 moments +' closed and 'BEHIND YOU 3 moments −' open; state=desk the same; state=day 'BEHIND YOU 9 moments +' / '−'. U+2212 is announced as 'minus'. This is the only control a guest is ever given on the received artifact, and its name ends in a stray 'plus' or 'minus' that duplicates, in the wrong grammar, the expanded state the DisclosureTriangle role already carries. It is also the one place in the lab where a decorative mark reaches the accessibility tree at all — every other presentational mark (.b-tick, .b-rail, .b-origin, the crowded leader) is correctly aria-hidden or pseudo-only, and render-core.js:micro() goes out of its way to keep uppercase out of the tree.
findings.fix: Use the alternative-text form of the content property so the glyph paints and the name does not: at b.css:432 write `content: "+" / "";` and at b.css:440 write `content: "\2212" / "";`. Supported in Chromium, Safari and Firefox; the rendered mark is byte-identical. Assertion to write first: in interaction-check.mjs, for states phone, desk and day on both grounds, read the summary's accessible name and require it to equal the concatenation of .b-behindLabel and .b-behindCount text with no trailing character.

findings.element: b.css:1555-1566 — @media (forced-colors: active) .b-item[data-lead="true"] .b-tick { border-width: 3px } vs .b-back .b-item[data-lead="true"] .b-tick { background: Canvas; border-color: CanvasText }
findings.problem: The forced-colours block carries its own comment at b.css:1559-1561: 'A forced palette may repaint any fill, so the mark that means "this one" is carried in geometry too - a ring nothing else has.' The geometry is border-width:3px plus border-style:solid on the lead tick. place() sets data-lead="true" on the first row of every measure including the past rail (render-b.js:353), and the reset at b.css:1566 restores background and border-colour but not border-width, so the 3px ring survives onto the past. Measured with forcedColors:active on state=day at 390, disclosure open, in both light and dark forced schemes: .b-back .b-item[data-lead="true"] .b-tick renders 7x7 with a 3px CanvasText solid border, every other past tick renders 7x7 with 1px. With box-sizing:border-box a 3px border on a 7px box leaves a 1px core, so the most recent thing that already happened becomes the heaviest, near-solid mark on the screen — carrying the exact geometry the block reserves for the next thing, on a rail where nothing is next. Neither gate reaches it: audit.mjs never emulates forced-colors, and interaction-check.mjs's past-rail block (line 2507-2531) does not either.
findings.fix: Complete the reset. At b.css:1566 change the rule to `.b-back .b-item[data-lead="true"] .b-tick { background: Canvas; border-color: CanvasText; border-width: 1px; }`. Assertion to write first: in interaction-check.mjs open a context with forcedColors 'active', load state=day, click .b-behindSummary, and require every .b-back .b-tick to report the same borderTopWidth.

biggestWin: The two grounds are one design rather than a theme, and it holds under measurement rather than under description. Everything downstream is written against --fore/--back, and the proof is that the ladders survive where the gates cannot look: a full scan of font-size, leading ratio, letterfit, weight, family and radius over surfaces that only exist after interaction — the empty project's second screen after the day is set, the past disclosure opened on phone and on the morning, loading-slow after Try again, the preview strip that only appears when the owner arrived by pressing Preview, the docked editor at 390 — returned zero off-ladder values on ?v=paper and zero on ?v=ink. The measure itself is the other half of it: position is the quantity, setAway is the only writer of a distance, every fact on the row is derived from the one date it computes in the same frame, and place() is a fixed point that re-groups before it measures. Driving the owner surface at 1440, 1279 and 390 on both grounds, every Edit control is reachable in nearest-first order, the pane scrolls each one into view as focus arrives, and the moment being moved stays inside the free band while the stepper under the hand does not move. That is Linear-grade plumbing, and it is why the four items above are corrections rather than rebuilds.
